Q: what is the difference between kotlin ..< operator and until operation for ranges A:

For integral types (Int, Long, Char, Byte), there is no difference at all. Both ..< and until produce ranges that are both ClosedRanges and also the new OpenRange type. But ..< can also be used with any other Comparable type to create specifically an OpenRange.

The KEEP design document states that Jetbrains conducted a study and found that misinterpretations of whether the range was inclusive or exclusive was reduced by about 20-30% when comparing until with ..<. So there is data supporting that mistakes are made and can be reduced, but we can only guess at the reasons people might misinterpret until.

I will not be surprised if they eventually deprecate until and remove it from the language. There is a general language design goal in Kotlin to avoid redundancies that lead to language bloat, which contributes to code being less readable overall.

Other than reducing errors in interpreting and writing code, the other benefits are the new OpenRange concept and the symmetry of using an operator for both closed and open ranges. Users often were typing out 1..(x - 1) even though convention preferred until, probably because of a desire for symmetry or because of familiarity with using an operator for it.

Q: Azure Devops handle special character in yaml A:

In the comments to the question the original poster stated that:

Solved it using single quote in the variable, like '$xxx'

This might seem surprising. But this is indeed the solution for an Ubuntu vmImage pool if and when the tasks run in bash. In bash both ' and " can be used for string literals.

Since they are using an Ubuntu pool, this means that script blocks and most tasks run will automatically run in a bash shell. Here is an example and the working result:

trigger:
- none

pool:
  vmImage: 'ubuntu-latest'

variables:
  staticVar: |
    Here are some special characters:  !&#%*" 

jobs:
- job: TestEcho
  steps:         
  - script: | 
      echo '${{variables.staticVar}}'

However it is not quite adequate because there is still an edge case that breaks it. What if the string itself contains the ' character (or " of you used that for the literal):

variables:
  staticVar:
    Here are some special characters:  A0!&#%*"'

Then the pipeline fails with:

/home/vsts/work/_temp/0e4c1722-cdc1-4dbe-9804-179ca8e18e4a.sh: line 3: unexpected EOF while looking for matching `'' 

##[error]Bash exited with code '2'. 

Finishing: CmdLine

This is because the ' character is being interpreted by bash.

When working directly in bash one would normally escape the ' by duplicating it: '' , or if using " as the literal one would escape with ""

So one might consider attempting to find and escape the ' character, piping it into a new variable:

processedVar=$(echo "${{variables.staticVar}}" | sed "s/'/'\"'\"'/g")

processedVar=$(sed -e "s/'/'\"'\"'/g" <<< ${{variables.staticVar}})

But in both cases bash will of course interpret special characters before this happens so these will fail.

A working solution is to use a heredoc, as mentioned in one of the answers here:
How to quote string of special characters?

Here is an example where I curl to an ftp server where the format of the curl command is curl -u username:password server
When writing a heredoc the 'EOF' and EOF must be on their own lines

trigger:
- none

pool:
  vmImage: 'ubuntu-latest'

variables:
  password: A0!&#%*"'

jobs:
- job: TestEcho

  steps:
  - script: |

      curl -u testuser2@redacted-servername.com:$(cat <<'EOF'
      ${{ variables.password }}
      EOF
      ) ftp://ftp.redacted-servername.com

Q: CONVERT or CAST in db2, how to convert a column from char to decimal A:

Your WHERE clause needs the conversion/cast.

Your example was:
select cast(date as varchar(10) from trans where date <> user

When I run into problems like this, I start out by inspecting the fields, and add my conversions as extra columns.

select date, cast(date as varchar(10) as date1, user from trans fetch first 10 rows only

In this case, you need to cast your date as part of the WHERE clause.

select date, user from trans where cast(date as varchar(10) <> user

SQL SELECT runs step-by-step (ignoring optimization):
- locate tables (FROM)
- filter records (WHERE )
- collect, calculate and convert data to return (SELECT)

Your cast of a result field (SELECT) did not alter the date <> user expression (WHERE).

I hope this helps!

Q: Unzip files with SQL A:

Others suggest you can use Powershell which would have been the only older native windows method for XP to early Windows 10.

But current Windows 10 and 11 have a command line unzipper in Tar.EXE. it is easy once you understand its oddities to unpack/update from local or web zip files etc. (for web.zip using curl)

Example general usage https://stackoverflow.com/a/70011759/10802527

OR say for download chrome headless shell try something like

set "download=chrome-headless-shell-win32.zip"
set "variant=win32/%download%"

curl -o LATEST_RELEASE_STABLE.txt https://googlechromelabs.github.io/chrome-for-testing/LATEST_RELEASE_STABLE
set /p version=<LATEST_RELEASE_STABLE.txt
curl -O https://storage.googleapis.com/chrome-for-testing-public/%version%/%variant%
tar -xf %download%

Usage is only limited by your ingenuity.

Q: using adb backup/restore? A:

When restoring, you need to enter the password that your phone had when you made the backup, because the backup is encrypted. If you don't enter the correct password, adb restore will terminate without warning.
